Neonates of the Sleepy Lizard (Tiliqua rugosa), a large-bodied scincid endemic to southern Australia, emerge with a snout to vent length of 16.5 centimeters [Lb = 16.5 centimeters] based on a sample of thirteen individuals from the Munns dataset, a size that reflects substantial maternal investment in each offspring and represents a surprisingly large proportion of the ultimate adult size. This considerable initial length indicates that post-natal growth, while sustained, does not involve the dramatic size increases seen in many other squamate reptiles, such as smaller agamid or gekkonid species. The timing of this emergence, or parturition event, is also well documented under natural thermal regimes; the gestation period, from conception through embryonic development to the birth of the yolk-sac larva, spans 150 days [ab = 150 days]. This protracted gestation is typical of large-bodied, viviparous skinks and is likely linked to the relatively cool active season temperatures encountered in the species' semi-arid and Mediterranean-climate range within Western Australia. The dry weight of these newly born individuals was recorded at 29.7 grams , derived from a sample of fifteen neonates, a value that underscores the considerable caloric investment each female makes per offspring and contributes to exceptionally high neonatal survival rates in the wild.

As individuals progress through their juvenile phase, a critical developmental milestone is the attainment of sexual maturity, observed to occur when they reach a snout to vent length of 23 centimeters [Lp = 23 centimeters]. This body size threshold, corresponding to the onset of puberty, represents a significant physiological transition, marking the point at which resources begin to be directed toward gametogenesis onset. Upon reaching this length, the typical dry body mass is estimated at 54 grams , a value derived from length-weight regressions from the Munns observations. Growth trajectories slow considerably after this point, as individuals begin to reallocate energetic resources from somatic expansion toward reproductive preparation. The age at which this first reproductive event occurs has been calculated as approximately 1.5 years after birth [tR = approximately 1.5 years after birth], a figure derived from field observations where a female was documented reproducing at three years of age, with adjustments made for the gestation period of her offspring and the time required to accumulate sufficient body condition for subsequent breeding. This relatively delayed first reproduction is consistent with the K-selected life-history strategy, favoring longevity and iteroparity over rapid, early maturation.

Adult female Sleepy Lizards attain a maximum snout to vent length of 32.8 centimeters [Li = 32.8 centimeters], representing the ultimate or asymptotic body size recorded in the Munns study population. At this upper size limit, the corresponding dry body mass reaches approximately 215.1 grams , a value averaged from a series of post-partum females captured over the course of the study. Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active season, approximately 23.2 degrees Celsius [T = 23.2 degrees Celsius], the maximum reproductive output is constrained by both clutch size and the interval between breeding events. Females typically produce a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], with each litter containing up to 3 offspring [N_R_i = each litter containing up to 3 offspring], yielding an annual maximum reproductive rate of 3 offspring per year. This modest fecundity, however, is compensated for by the large body size and high survival rates of the newborns, as well as the extended reproductive lifespan of the adults.

Longevity data for the Sleepy Lizard indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7,629 days [am = approximately 7,629 days] under captive conditions, with field studies suggesting that wild individuals may li at a temperature of 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C]ve even longer. Bauer reported a maximum of 13.6 years based on captive specimens, while field researchers, including Kearney, Moritz, and Roberts, recaptured an individual at Paynes Find Station that had been originally marked 15 years earlier as an adult, suggesting that individuals may regularly surpass the 20-year mark in undisturbed habitats. This extended lifespan, coupled with the late age at first reproduction of 1.5 years after birth [tR = 1.5 years after birth], places Tiliqua rugosa firmly among the slow-lived end of the squamate life-history continuum. The trade-off between high adult survival and low annual fecundity is a classic signature of a bet-hedging strategy, well-suited to the unpredictable rainfall and resource availability of the semi-arid and Mediterranean-climate regions they inhabit. The substantial dry weight at birth, nearly 30 grams (29.7 grams) , also contributes to high neonate survival, further reinforcing this slow-paced life cycle.

Comparative studies with other large-bodied scincids reveal that the growth parameters of the Sleepy Lizard are broadly consistent with a slow life-history strategy. The snout to vent length at birth of 16.5 centimeters [Lb = 16.5 centimeters] is exceptionally large relative to maternal body size among viviparous skinks, providing offspring with a significant survival advantage. The 150-day gestation period (150 days) [ab = 150 days] is among the longest recorded for any Australian skink, reflecting the cool thermal environment and the slow metabolic rates typical of this member of the family Scincidae. Furthermore, the attainment of sexual maturity at 23 centimeters [Lp = 23 centimeters] snout to vent length and a dry mass of 54 grams  occurs relatively late compared to many smaller skinks, but is consistent with the overall slow pace of life. Recent analyses suggest that the species' maximum reproductive rate can be expressed as approximately 0.0024 offspring per day based on its source data, though field observations have recorded annual outputs of 3 offspring per year [Ri = 3 offspring per year] and one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. This low fecundity is offset by the exceptional adult survival rates and long reproductive lifespans, which together ensure a stable population turnover.
